segments.title: Opening: The Fog and the Law

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of Charles Dickens's great novel about fog, law, and the people the system grinds down.
I'm your host, and over this series we'll be moving through the novel chapter by chapter — its characters, its language, and the world it both describes and indicts.
Three experts join me today, each bringing a genuinely distinct lens to the book.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and who argues that Dickens was more radical than even Dickens knew.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — the person in the room who can tell you exactly what the Court of Chancery was, what it cost, and what it did to people.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read Bleak House many times over — someone who loves to read it aloud and has strong views about which characters deserve better.
Today we're opening the novel — the fog, the law, and the first impressions of Bleak House itself.
Let's begin with Caroline — because Dickens gives us, early on, a vision of warmth and domesticity that feels almost deliberately placed against everything dark in the novel.
The first thing I want to say about Bleak House — the house itself, not the novel — is that it surprises you.
You arrive expecting something grim, given the name.
And what Esther finds is this extraordinarily alive, slightly eccentric, deeply comfortable place.
The details Dickens gives us are genuinely funny — birds in paintings staring at a stuffed trout, portraits of the same person split between different rooms.
But then Esther gathers all of it into this one long, almost breathless sentence that I think is one of the most beautiful in the novel.
She writes:

"with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House"
That phrase — "just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment" — that's music.
Dickens is writing the whole scene as if it has a score.
And of course the novel will test that warmth against everything that lies outside it — the fog, the court, the suffering.
James, you wanted to bring in one of the novel's darker registers — the ghost story that haunts the Dedlock family.
Yes — and I think Caroline is right that there's warmth here, real warmth.
But Dickens is also constructing, in these early chapters, a very deliberate counterpoint.
Set against that domestic warmth, you have Chesney Wold — the Dedlock estate — and its ghost.
Not a metaphorical ghost — a literal family curse, delivered by a crippled woman dying on the terrace.
Dickens gives her words of extraordinary, cold force.

"I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!"
Now — what is that, sociologically?
It's the repressed — literally written out of the family history — returning to threaten the pride of a great house.
Dickens wraps it in gothic dressing, but the structural logic is perfectly clear.
What strikes me is how much work the word "pride" is doing there.
The Dedlocks are the apex of the class structure Dickens is mapping — landed gentry, ancient name, political influence.
And the novel will dismantle them — systematically, almost surgically.
But the instrument of their humbling isn't revolution — it's the same Court of Chancery that destroys the poor.
Which is where Gridley comes in — and he is, I think, the most politically unambiguous character in these early chapters.
He announces himself with a kind of terrible dignity.
"I have been dragged for five and twenty years over burning iron, and I have lost the habit of treading upon velvet."
That contrast — burning iron against velvet — is the whole novel in miniature.
Those at the bottom are scorched. Those at the top walk softly. The law makes no distinction.
And Gridley's line about being "the man from Shropshire" — a standing joke in the Court — is historically exact.
Chancery litigants were notorious figures — people consumed by cases that ran for decades, becoming objects of ridicule rather than sympathy.
The Court didn't just ruin you financially — it made you a joke.
It stripped you of dignity while professing to serve justice.
That is not a polemical exaggeration on Dickens's part — that is what the record shows.
What moves me about the Gridley passage is the apology buried inside it.
He pauses his fury to say "I beg your pardon" — twice — before going right back to the burning iron.
He hasn't lost his manners. He's just lost the belief that manners will be reciprocated.
And that, I think, is Dickens at his most precise — not raging on behalf of his characters, but letting you hear exactly what twenty-five years of injustice sounds like.
Fog and law, warmth and ruin — and already in these opening chapters the novel is holding all of it at once.
In our next segment, we'll look at how Dickens's two narrators — Esther and the omniscient voice — divide that world between them.

segments.title: Richard's Long Decline: Ambition and Ruin

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We're exploring one of the novel's most quietly devastating storylines: the slow ruin of Richard Carstone.
Richard begins the novel as a charming, restless young man full of possibility — and Dickens watches him unravel with pitiless precision.
With me today are Daniel Rosen, Caroline Woodcourt, and James Blackstone.
Daniel reads Dickens as a diagnostician of class and institutional power — and Richard's story, as we'll hear, is very much a story about what institutions do to people.
Caroline has lived with this novel for decades and brings a close reader's eye to Dickens's extraordinary verbal craft.
And James brings the legal and social historian's perspective — what it actually meant, in mid-Victorian England, to be young, uncertain, and entangled in Chancery.
Let's start at the beginning of Richard's arc — that early scene in Chapter Thirteen where he and Ada declare their love and Mr. Jarndyce offers his counsel.
What strikes me every time I re-read those early chapters is how tenderly Dickens frames Richard and Ada's love — and how immediately he shadows it.
Esther describes the three of them sitting together, Richard and Ada on either side of her, confiding like children.
And then she gives us this passage that I find almost unbearably moving in retrospect.
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
That parenthetical — "I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself" — is so characteristic of Esther.
She steps aside from the warmth just long enough to let us feel it fully.
And then she tells us it could only come to happiness if it inspired them with constancy, fortitude, perseverance — each always for the other's sake.
We know, of course, what will happen to Richard's constancy.
And Jarndyce sees it coming — that's what's remarkable about his counsel in Chapter Thirteen.
He doesn't simply bless their love; he tries to arm Richard against the very thing that will destroy him.
The speech is almost a diagnosis delivered in advance.
Listen to what he actually says to Richard:
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
And then, more pointedly:
"Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort."
Jarndyce is not counselling patience — he is counselling labour, active engagement, the refusal of magical thinking.
And Richard, of course, will do the opposite — he will wait on Chancery to deliver him.
Which tells us something important about the structural trap Richard falls into.
Jarndyce's advice is sound, but it presupposes that Richard has a viable world of effort to enter.
What Chancery actually does — and this is historically documented — is create dependency.
Suitors became psychologically and financially tethered to proceedings that could last decades.
The system made it rational — if you can call it that — to defer ordinary life, because the suit might resolve everything tomorrow.
Jarndyce understands this; Richard cannot, yet.
And the scene that follows — Esther watching them walk through the sunlit room — makes that foreboding almost physical.
That passage is one of the most quietly devastating things in the entire novel, and I don't think it ever gets enough attention.
Dickens sets it up so simply: the door stands open, and Esther watches them move away through a sunlit room.
Richard's head bent, Ada's hand drawn through his arm, listening, seeming to see nothing else.
And then Esther gives us this:

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
Three sentences. And the whole novel's tragic arc is already written.
It's a Gothic signal delivered in naturalistic prose — which is exactly Dickens's method.
The sun clouds over. It's a weather event. And it's also a prophecy.
But what I want to insist on is that Richard's decline is not simply personal weakness — the Court collaborates in his destruction.
Jarndyce offers the right advice, but the system Richard is embedded in makes that advice almost impossible to follow.
And what makes Dickens radical is that he shows us both: the individual's failure and the structure that enabled it.
That structural reading becomes even sharper when you look at Richard's medical interlude in Chapter Seventeen.
Mrs. Badger delivers what is essentially a professional assessment of Richard — and it's brutal in its accuracy.
She tells Esther that Richard lacks the positive interest in medicine that makes it a vocation.
And then she contrasts him directly with Woodcourt:

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
The contrast is devastating precisely because it isn't melodramatic.
Mrs. Badger isn't condemning Richard; she's simply observing him clearly, without sentiment.
And Dickens uses her social register — the drawing-room manner — to make the diagnosis land all the harder.
What I find so painful about that scene is the implicit comparison with Woodcourt — who will later prove himself in exactly the ways Richard never manages.
Mrs. Badger's phrase — "his vocation" — carries enormous weight in a novel so concerned with people finding their right purpose.
Richard drifts from medicine to law to the army — each time, slightly more hollowed out.
And Dickens never lets us forget that Chancery is the undertow dragging at him through each of those careers.
It's worth pausing here on what the novel sets alongside Richard's decline — because it's not incidental.
In Chapter Eight, we get the brickmaker's scene — one of the most unsparing passages in Dickens.
Mrs. Pardiggle arrives with her clipboard-philanthropy, and the man on the floor simply detonates it.
He anticipates every question she's going to ask and answers them himself, without mercy:
"Is my daughter a-washin? Yes, she IS a-washin. Look at the water. Smell it! That's wot we drinks."

"An't my place dirty? Yes, it is dirty — it's nat'rally dirty, and it's nat'rally onwholesome; and we've had five dirty and onwholesome children, as is all dead infants, and so much the better for them, and for us besides."
This man is not a sentimental victim — he is a structural fact.
Dickens puts him in the novel to show us what the system actually produces — not Richard's romantic ruin, but this.
The brickmaker's speech is one of the most historically precise things in the novel.
Every detail he names — the water, the gin, the dead children, the church beadle's gentility — is documented in the blue books of the 1840s and 50s.
And the point about charitable intervention is crucial: he refuses to be drawn like a badger.
That phrase — "drawed like a badger" — refers to the practice of baiting: the poor being prodded for sport and edification.
Mrs. Pardiggle's philanthropy is indistinguishable, in his experience, from harassment.
And Dickens gives him the rhetorical victory — completely, unambiguously.
What I find striking is how the brickmaker's speech is constructed — the relentless accumulation, the self-interrogation.
He performs Mrs. Pardiggle's questions before she can ask them, turning her method against her.
It's theatrically brilliant — and it's also the only power available to him.
Richard has choices — profession, patronage, the suit itself — however corrupted those choices become.
This man has nothing but his capacity to refuse the narrative others would impose on him.
Exactly — and that juxtaposition is what makes Bleak House a genuinely radical novel, rather than merely a reformist one.
Richard's tragedy is rendered with compassion and psychological depth.
But Dickens insists we hold it alongside a man whose tragedy has no psychological depth to speak of — only material fact.
Five dead children. Water you wouldn't wash in. A wife with a black eye.
Dickens knew that the novel form tended to privilege the inner life of the relatively comfortable — and he kept straining against that tendency.
That tension — between the intimate tragedy of a character we know and the structural tragedy of one we barely meet — sits at the very heart of the novel's ambition.
Jarndyce warns Richard that love means nothing without effort; the brickmaker demonstrates what a world without genuine opportunity looks like.
And Dickens holds both truths in the same novel, refusing to let either one excuse the other.
In our next segment, we'll be following Esther herself — the novel's most contested narrator — and asking what her particular form of self-erasure costs her, and costs us.

segments.title: A System Built on Suffering: Jo and the Streets

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel seriously — all of it, the darkness and the wit and the structural fury.
I'm your host, and today we're going deep into one of the novel's most devastating territories: the way the system grinds its most vulnerable people into nothing.
We have three guests with us, each bringing a sharply different lens to the text.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads institutions — the law, philanthropy, the courts — as mechanisms of class power.
He will be asking, as he always does, who benefits and who pays.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows what these institutions actually were — not just as literary devices, but as lived realities for the people caught inside them.

And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read Bleak House more times than most of us have had hot dinners, and who brings the reader's eye — the ear — to what the prose is doing sentence by sentence.
We begin with the novel's underclass — with Nemo dying in his garret, and with Jo, the crossing-sweeper, who may be the most heartbreaking figure Dickens ever put on a page.
Daniel, you've been assigned the passages that cluster around Nemo's death and Jo's testimony at the inquest. Where do you want to start?
I want to start with the room, because the room is the argument.
Tulkinghorn enters and sees Nemo — and what Dickens gives us is not a man, not yet, but an accumulation of material conditions.
Listen to how the description layers: a low bed, dirty patchwork, lean-ribbed ticking, coarse sacking.
Every noun is a verdict on what this society provides for its most desperate people.
And then Dickens lands his real blow — not visual but sensory.
"Through the general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco, there comes into the lawyer's mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium."
The taste enters Tulkinghorn's mouth — the lawyer's mouth — and he does nothing with it.
That's the system in miniature: it can perceive suffering with perfect clarity, and then proceed without interruption.
What strikes me about that passage — and I've read it many times — is the candle.
Dickens writes that its wick has doubled over and left a tower of winding-sheet above it.
A winding-sheet is a burial shroud.
The candle is already laying out its own corpse before anyone in the room acknowledges what they're looking at.
Dickens is working with a kind of compressed poetry here — every object in the room is morally weighted.
And the man at the centre of it all is described through negatives — ragged, neglected, grown like scum.
He has been defined entirely by what he has been denied.
The context here matters enormously, and I think it sharpens what both of you are saying.
Opium in 1850s London was not a romantic vice — it was a poor person's painkiller and sedative, cheap and freely sold.
It was the recourse of people in chronic pain who had no access to medicine, no sick leave, no welfare provision of any kind.
So when that taste reaches Tulkinghorn's mouth, Dickens is not giving us a Gothic shudder — he is giving us a precise social fact.
And then, of course, Tulkinghorn does absolutely nothing about it.
That's exactly right — and Dickens gives Tulkinghorn a kind of negative definition that's almost philosophical.
He has shown neither patience nor impatience, nor attention nor abstraction.
"He has shown nothing but his shell."
And then comes the image that I keep returning to.
"As easily might the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case, as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case."
The man is a container with no detectable interior.
And that, for Dickens, is not a personality quirk — it is the perfect institutional type.
The musical instrument simile is extraordinary, isn't it.
It's elegant — it sounds almost like a compliment — and then you realise it's the most damning thing you can say about a human being.
You cannot know what music he might make, because the case is all you ever see.
James's point about Tulkinghorn doing nothing lands even harder when you read that image — he is structurally incapable of being moved.
And from the man who processes death without feeling, we move to the boy who barely exists in the eyes of the law at all.
Daniel, Jo's testimony at the inquest — tell us about that passage.
This is, for my money, one of the most radical passages in Victorian fiction.
Dickens presents Jo's testimony as a kind of inventory of negation.
The prose strips everything away one item at a time.
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Four nouns removed.
Dickens is counting what the system has withheld from this child, and presenting the bill publicly, in court, through a legal form that was designed precisely to exclude people like Jo.
And then — this is what makes me angrier each time — Jo is eventually dismissed as an incompetent witness because he can't swear on the Bible.
The system that denied him education then disqualifies him for lacking it.
And that detail is historically precise, which is what makes Dickens so devastating here.
Witnesses in Victorian coroner's courts were required to understand the nature of an oath — which meant, in practice, a Christian understanding of divine punishment.
Jo doesn't pass that test, but — and this is crucial — Dickens makes him pass a different test entirely.
Listen to what Jo does know.
"Knows a broom's a broom, and knows it's wicked to tell a lie."
He has a morality — arrived at without instruction, without institution, without any of the apparatus the respectable classes consider essential.
Dickens is inverting the court's logic: the boy with nothing knows what the court, apparently, does not.
What I find unbearable about this passage — in the best sense — is its rhythm.
Dickens writes it in a kind of staccato third-person ventriloquism.
Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on.
"Don't know that everybody has two names. Never heerd of sich a think."
The spelling — heerd, sich, think — isn't mockery.
It's transcription — Dickens is insisting that you hear the actual voice of this child, not a cleaned-up literary version of it.
And the question — what's home? — with no answer following it.
That blank is the whole novel.

Caroline's point about the blank connects to something I want to raise about where the novel takes us later — because Dickens doesn't let the powerful entirely off the hook either, even where we might expect him to.
There's a passage late in the novel, when Sir Leicester's pride has been broken by the exposure of Lady Dedlock's secret.
And Dickens writes something that feels almost like a concession — almost like hope.
"In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."
It's a genuinely radical equalising image — a baronet and a crossing-sweeper made of the same material.
But I'd argue that line only lands because of everything the novel has shown us about Jo.
You can only believe in shared humanity when you've looked at what the system does to those it abandons.
I find that passage moving, but I want to push back slightly on the word hope.
Children of the dust shine equally — yes.
But dust is what you return to.
The equality Dickens is gesturing at here is an equality in death, in shared mortality — not in life chances, not in social provision, not in anything the state might actually do.
Jo gets nothing in this world.
James, that's right — and yet I keep coming back to the fact that Dickens puts it there at all.
He is insisting that Sir Leicester's grief is honourable — his noble earnestness, his fidelity, his generous conquest of his own wrong.
Those are qualities Dickens genuinely admires, even in a man whose class the novel otherwise indicts.
That tension — the novel's refusal to make the aristocracy simply monstrous — is part of what makes Bleak House so hard to summarise politically.
Daniel's right that Jo is the measuring stick.
Everything else in the novel is judged by what it does — or refuses to do — for the child with one name and no address.
That image — one name, no address — crystallises something we'll be returning to throughout this episode.

Before we move on, I want to pick up the thread of secrecy and surveillance — because running alongside Jo's total exposure is a very different kind of invisibility, one inhabited by Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn.
James, you've been looking at the passage where Dickens describes their silent war — the way they meet day after day, perfectly masked.
Yes — and this passage offers perhaps the starkest contrast with everything we've been saying about Jo.
Jo has no concealment available to him.
His poverty, his illiteracy, his parentlessness — all of it is on public display at the inquest for the coroner's amusement.
Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn, by contrast, are locked in a private performance of perfect social normality.
Dickens puts it with characteristic precision.
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
The performance is total.
And it has to be total, because the stakes — for her — are everything.
What I find striking is the symmetry Dickens creates between Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock here.
Both are performing — but for radically different reasons.
She performs to survive.
He performs — or rather, refuses to perform — to accumulate power.
And Dickens captures that mutual watchfulness with a sentence I think of as the novel's most forensic.
"Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares."
That word evermore — used three times — it's relentless.
This is the cold war at the heart of the aristocratic world.
And what Dickens adds, after all of that, is the sentence that quietly destroys you.
"What each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
For the time.
Those two words carry the whole menace of the novel.
Nothing is safely hidden forever.
For the time — and the time, of course, will run out.

We've moved today from the dying body of Nemo in his garret, through the stripped testimony of Jo at the inquest, and into the sealed chambers of power where Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn wage their silent war.
What connects them is what Daniel named at the start: a system that perceives suffering clearly and then proceeds.
My thanks to Daniel Rosen, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt.
We'll be back shortly with our next segment.

segments.title: Lady Dedlock's Shadow: Secrets and Recognition

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great social novel apart — slowly, carefully, and with genuine pleasure.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the novel's most intricately plotted tensions — the shadow that falls over Lady Dedlock.
Secrets — kept, suspected, and nearly revealed — are the atmosphere this novel breathes, much like the fog that opens it.
Three brilliant readers are with me today to help us navigate it.
Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in this novel as a machine for concentrating power — and he's going to show us exactly how the law operates here.
James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who can tell us what Chancery and the men who served it actually meant in Dickens's England — and in ours.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived inside this novel for decades and never stopped noticing new things in the prose.
Welcome, all three of you.
Let's begin where the novel itself begins — with that extraordinary fog.
I have re-read that opening more times than I can count, and it still stops me cold.
Dickens doesn't ease you in — he drops you straight into the fog as though you were already lost in it.
The repetition is the point — every iteration of that word is a new place it reaches, a new life it smothers.
Listen to the way he builds it — from the grand sweep of rivers to something almost unbearably small.
"Fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of his shivering little 'prentice boy on deck."
That word — cruelly — is doing so much work.
The fog isn't passive weather — it has intent.
And by the time we reach Lady Dedlock, we already know: no one escapes it.
What strikes me about that fog passage is the social precision underneath the poetry.
The fog reaches everyone — but it doesn't reach them equally.
The pensioner wheezes by a fireside, the skipper sits in his cabin — and the apprentice boy is exposed on deck.
Hierarchy is reproduced even inside a fog.
And that's the lens we need when we turn to Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn.
Tulkinghorn is the fog made human — he penetrates every space, and what he carries is not weather but knowledge weaponised as class power.
That's precisely right, and Dickens nails something real about the legal profession of the period.
A family solicitor like Tulkinghorn wasn't merely an employee of the great houses — he was their indispensable secret-keeper.
Which meant the information he held was leverage — whether he chose to use it openly or not.
Dickens captures this ambiguity with forensic care.
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret."
We genuinely don't know if Tulkinghorn serves these people out of loyalty or contempt.
And that uncertainty is, in itself, a form of power over them.
The prose of that description does something I find almost unsettling — it's in third person but it thinks like Tulkinghorn.
The narrator can't get inside him, so it describes the surface — the pace, the mask — and then poses questions it cannot answer.
"He wears his usual expressionless mask — if it be a mask."
That parenthetical — if it be a mask — is the whole problem.
What if it isn't a mask at all?
What if that blankness is simply what he is?
That's chilling precisely because it has a structural answer.
The system doesn't require Tulkinghorn to have feelings about what he does.
He carries family secrets in every crease of his dress — that's not metaphor, that's a job description.
And watch what he does with those secrets when he finally delivers his message to Sir Leicester.
He routes it through the husband — in a letter, read aloud, in the wife's presence.
The social performance of that delivery is as controlled as his pace on the terrace.
And Sir Leicester's performance of reading it is exquisite — or rather, his performance of fumbling.
He takes forever to find his eyeglass, to locate the passage — while Lady Dedlock waits, looking, as the narrator notes, a little irritated.
That irritation is the first crack in the composure Dickens has been building in her.
Then the message finally arrives.
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Three words at the end: I have seen him.
In the Victorian legal world, information about an illegitimate child could end a woman's social existence entirely.
Those three words are a loaded pistol, laid gently on the table.
And Lady Dedlock's response — what is her response?
That's what makes the scene so extraordinary — it's barely there.
Dickens gives us this extended look at what the two of them are doing beneath the surface.
"During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another."
Customary deportment — sustained through a moment that is anything but customary.
The social armour holds, and that's almost more frightening than if it had broken.
And then Dickens does something formally very bold — he steps back entirely from what the characters know.
He poses the question as unanswerable — which is itself the point.

"Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation... what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
Hidden, for the time — that conditional phrase is doing enormous work.
The secret won't stay hidden — the novel has already told us that.
What's chilling is not the revelation to come but the perfectly maintained surface right now.
There's something worth noting about the one figure who doesn't watch at all — Sir Leicester, looking at the fire.
"Sir Leicester has looked at the fire, with the general expression of the Dedlock on the staircase."
The Dedlock on the staircase — meaning the portrait, the ancestral type.
Sir Leicester isn't just a character; he's become a symbol of his own class's vacancy.
He trusts to hear no more about the matter — because it is beneath the dignity of a Dedlock to have such associations.
The class system protecting itself by refusing, on principle, to look.
Which brings us, finally, to Esther — to what this secret means for the young woman at its other end.
When Jarndyce finally tells her what he knows of her origins, the language is almost unbearably restrained.
He's describing a resolution someone else has made about Esther's entire existence — and she has no say in it whatsoever.
The phrasing tells you everything about the power at work here.
"That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
For any human consideration — that phrase is terrible in its absoluteness.
Including, presumably, the consideration of Esther herself.
And notice the mechanism that keeps it all in place — the confidential agent, the assumed name, the refusal to be seen.
Secrecy, in this novel, is never personal — it's institutional.
The law administers it, the aristocracy requires it, the family solicitor enforces it.
Esther is not kept in ignorance because one woman is ashamed — she's kept in ignorance because the whole structure depends on it.
There it is — the personal and the political fused in a single withheld name.
The fog that opens the novel doesn't stay outside — it's inside every institution, every silence, every letter read aloud to the wrong person.
Daniel, James, Caroline — that was a remarkable reading of how Dickens builds his architecture of concealment.
We'll be back shortly to look at what happens when that architecture begins to crack.

segments.title: Laughter and Darkness: Dickens's Comic Mercy

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's great novel apart to see how it breathes.
I'm your host, and today we're asking a question that cuts to the heart of what makes this novel so extraordinary.
How does Dickens hold the comedy and the darkness in the same hand — and why does it matter that he does?
With me today are three people who have thought long and hard about this book.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and who believes Dickens was more radical than he himself knew.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who can tell you exactly what Chancery was and why it was so devastating — and he does so with a wonderful dry wit.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read Bleak House more times than perhaps anyone should admit — and loves nothing more than a great Dickens sentence read aloud.
Caroline, let's start with you — and with the very first page.
Every time I return to that opening, I'm stopped cold.
Dickens doesn't begin with a character, or a plot — he begins with weather, and mud, and a kind of cosmic joke.
And then he drops this extraordinary sentence on us.

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
A dinosaur. Waddling. Up Holborn Hill.
It's absurd, and it's sublime, and it's both at exactly the same moment.
That's the Dickens trick — the comedy isn't relief from the darkness, it's made of the same material.
What strikes me about that passage is what's underneath the joke.
The mud isn't just atmosphere — it's accumulation.
Dickens actually uses the phrase "compound interest" — for mud, for sediment.
The city's filth is described in the language of capital.
The laugh is real — the Megalosaurus is genuinely funny.
But the world it inhabits is one where people are losing their footing — literally, in that opening — and the system grinds on regardless.
And of course it's November — Michaelmas term just ended.
The law has done its seasonal business and retreated, and this is what it leaves behind.
Fog, mud, ill temper, and foot passengers slipping on the crust of everyone who went before them.
The joke about the Megalosaurus works partly because it slots so naturally into a city that already feels prehistoric.
The institutions haven't changed since the dinosaurs, so why would the streets?
James, that's it exactly — the joke is also the diagnosis.
And Dickens returns to that mode again and again in the novel — comic grotesque that suddenly opens onto something chilling.
The Snagsby marriage is my favourite example.
Mrs. Snagsby's jealousy is played for comedy — she is absurd, she is relentless.
And then Dickens suddenly shifts the register with this passage.
"And henceforth he begins, go where he will, to be attended by another shadow than his own, hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his own."
"For the watchful Mrs. Snagsby is there too — bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow."
That Biblical echo — bone of his bone — turns a comic surveillance into something almost metaphysical.
It stopped being funny in the best possible way.
The shadow language is doing double work there.
On the surface, Mrs. Snagsby is comic — the suspicious, jealous wife.
But Snagsby is genuinely entangled in the novel's secrets — he does have things to hide, even if not what she suspects.
So her surveillance becomes a grotesque parody of the actual surveillance that runs through the whole novel.
Bucket watches everyone. Tulkinghorn watches Lady Dedlock. Mrs. Snagsby watches Snagsby.
The comedy spreads the surveillance down the class ladder — and that's a very precise satirical move.
And it's worth saying that the law produces this surveillance culture, not just mirrors it.
Dickens makes that case absolutely explicitly at one point — no irony, no metaphor.
Just the bluntest possible statement of what the system is for.
"The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself."
No other principle, he says, is distinctly, certainly, and consistently maintained through all its narrow turnings.
It's funny because it's so bald. And devastating because it's true.
The comedy and the horror share a sentence, share a full stop.
That's what I'd call Dickens's mercy, paradoxically.
He makes us laugh so that we can bear to look at what he's showing us.
And nowhere is that clearer than in the Smallweed scenes — the whole family is monstrous and magnificently funny at once.
Mr. Bucket, describing them to Jarndyce, achieves something almost like poetry.
"First the avaricious grandchildren split upon him on account of their objections to his living so unreasonably long, and then they split on one another."
"Lord! There ain't one of the family that wouldn't sell the other for a pound or two, except the old lady — and she's only out of it because she's too weak in her mind to drive a bargain."
"Too weak in her mind to drive a bargain" — that clause is a whole world.
It's funny and it's terrible and it's entirely, precisely Dickens.
Bucket's voice in that passage is worth dwelling on.
He's amused — genuinely, professionally amused — by human venality.
And that amusement is itself a form of power.
He knows which families betray each other and why — because that knowledge is his instrument.
So the comedy in that whispered aside is also Bucket exercising control, reducing the Smallweeds to a kind of anthropological exhibit.
And yet the document they're all squabbling over is a will in Jarndyce — which means it may change nothing and everything simultaneously.
Dickens understood that legal documents — singed, stained, nearly lost to fire — have this quality of terrible and absurd importance.
The Smallweeds' venality is comic, but it also shows you exactly how these documents move — through blackmail, through avarice, through family betrayal.
The law generates paper, the paper generates conflict, and conflict generates more business for the law.
Dickens's one great principle playing out in miniature.
What's remarkable is how that comic register can shift without warning into something genuinely haunting.
The Smallweed farce and the bleakness of Chesney Wold — they belong to the same novel, and somehow to the same breath.
George Rouncewell moving through that great empty house — holding his light up, thinking of the murdered man, the vanished Lady Dedlock — it's the comedy's shadow self.
Dickens gives us the jokes so that the silences land harder.
In our next segment, we'll look at the characters who bear the system's full weight — and ask what Dickens wants us to feel about them.

segments.title: Institutions and Injustice: The Chancery Haunts

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart, chapter by chapter, to ask what it really means — and why it still matters.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at one of the novel's great obsessions: the way institutions — the law, the aristocracy, the social machinery — grind people down and protect the powerful.
With me are three guests who know this novel with the kind of intimacy it rewards.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and Bleak House, he argues, is the most mercilessly clear-eyed of them all.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he knows what Chancery actually was, what the law actually did, and he's not inclined to soften it.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since adolescence — she reads it with the ear of someone who hears every note Dickens plays.
Daniel, I want to start with you — because Dickens opens a fascinating window onto the aristocracy in these early chapters, and it's not quite the window you might expect.
Yes — and what makes it so wickedly precise is that Dickens doesn't attack the aristocracy by showing them as tyrants.
He shows them as dupes. Managed, measured, led around by their own vanity.
Lady Dedlock believes herself to be, in the narrator's phrase, an inscrutable Being — quite out of the reach and ken of ordinary mortals.
And yet every dim little star revolving about her — from her maid to the manager of the Italian Opera — knows her weaknesses, prejudices, follies, haughtinesses, and caprices.
Every tradesperson, every flatterer — they all run their calculations on her moral nature as precisely as her dressmaker takes her physical proportions.
That parallel — moral nature, physical proportions — is devastating. The aristocracy is a body to be measured and dressed.
And then comes the Gulliver image — which is where it tips from satire into something almost structural.
Dickens writes that these tradespeople, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience, lead her and her whole troop after them —
who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput.
The aristocracy is the Lilliputian fleet: miniature, pompous, entirely unaware it is being towed.
That image is doing more than comic work, I think.
Blaze and Sparkle, Sheen and Gloss — these aren't incidental comic names. They're a specific class of commercial operators who existed precisely to monetize aristocratic prestige.
And Dickens gives them dialogue — the direct speech of commerce — which is quite unusual for his narrator.
Sheen and Gloss tell their manufacturer friends: you must come to us, because we know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it fashionable.
That word — make — carries a whole theory of social reality. Fashion isn't discovered; it's manufactured and sold back to those who fund it.
What's historically accurate here is that the great Victorian department stores and luxury mercers operated exactly on this logic of exclusive access.
The aristocracy provided legitimacy; the trade provided product; and the middlemen — your Mr. Sladdery — provided the circuit between the two.
What I keep noticing is how Dickens plays this completely straight — the narrator says Mr. Sladdery is an honest man and does not exaggerate at all.
Which is a perfect joke. Because Sladdery is bragging — I can turn them round my finger — and being confirmed as truthful makes it so much more damning.
The comedy and the critique are inseparable here. You laugh, and then you feel a little uncomfortable about having laughed.
But what strikes me most about this passage is the phrase 'nurse her all their lives.' It strips the aristocracy of any dignity or agency — they are infants in the hands of their own tradespeople.
Daniel, the novel doesn't let that satirical distance last very long, does it? Because in Chapter Eleven, we arrive somewhere very different — the inquest over the man known as Nemo.
And with him comes Jo — perhaps the novel's most devastating figure. What is Dickens doing with this pairing?
What the inquest scene does — and it's brutal — is place two kinds of excluded people in the same frame and ask what society has made of them.
Nemo is legally invisible in death — no name, no history, no witness admitted. Jo is legally invisible in life — too ignorant to swear an oath, his testimony inadmissible.
And yet the one real human connection the novel gives either of them is the relationship between these two men — the pauper boy and the nameless dead man.
Listen to how Dickens renders Nemo's approach to Jo. When the boy was shivering in a doorway, the man came back, and having questioned him and found that he had not a friend in the world, said —
Neither have I. Not one! and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
That 'Not one!' lands like a stone. Because it's recognition — the dead man sees himself in Jo. They are the same category of human being in the eyes of the system.
And yet within that mutual exclusion, there is an act of grace that the law refuses to acknowledge because Jo cannot be a witness.
The procedural detail there is worth pausing on. Jo is turned away as a witness because he cannot state what will be done to him for taking a false oath — meaning he lacks religious comprehension.
This was a genuine legal bar in mid-Victorian England. The Oaths Act didn't fully resolve it until 1869.
So Dickens isn't inventing this degradation. He's reporting it, with perfect accuracy, and then asking the reader to sit with the obscenity of it.
The coroner dismisses Jo. The narrator does not. He turns directly to the boy and says —
There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'
The misspelling — 'wos,' 'wery' — is not condescension. It's fidelity. Dickens renders Jo's voice exactly as it sounds and treats it as morally sufficient evidence.
The law excludes him. The novel includes him. That's the argument Dickens is making.
And the passage about Nemo before all of this — it's extraordinary, and people sometimes pass over it because it comes in the middle of a scene that's partly comic.
The jingling piano falls silent. The Harmonic friends go to bed. And Dickens turns to the body in the dark room and asks a question.
He imagines Nemo as a child at his mother's breast — eyes upraised to her loving face, soft hand scarcely knowing how to close upon the neck to which it crept.
And then: where is she, while these ashes are above the ground!
That exclamation mark — it isn't surprise. It's accusation. Where is she? And why has the world made it impossible to know?
We know — as Dickens knows we know — that Lady Dedlock is that mother. So this passage is doing something almost unbearable: it holds the satirical Lady Dedlock and the dead Nemo in the same grief.
The class that is managed and flattered and led by tradespeople — she is also the woman whose child died in the dark alone. That is the novel's full range, right there.
Caroline is right — and it complicates what I was saying about Lady Dedlock earlier. The satire doesn't cancel the tragedy. They coexist.
What the system does — what Chancery does, what the class structure does — is atomize people. It separates that mother from that child. It keeps them from finding each other.
And the Mrs. Piper scene — I want to bring that in, because it's easy to laugh at and easy to dismiss.
Mrs. Piper testifies that the deceased — and Dickens is brilliant here, because she insists on calling the dead man the plaintive — was reported to have sold himself.
the plaintive — so Mrs. Piper insists on calling the deceased — was reported to have sold himself.
The comic misprision — 'plaintive' for 'plaintiff' — doesn't just mock Mrs. Piper's ignorance. It reveals something about how the law sounds to those outside it.
The law is a foreign language to the poor. They mishear it, they misrepeat it — and the rumor that a man 'sold himself' is what fills the vacuum where legal identity should be.
That is exactly right. And it's worth saying that the inquest itself is the system's last chance to acknowledge Nemo's existence — and it fails him completely.
Jo's testimony — the only testimony that could tell us anything true about this man — is thrown out.
What replaces it is Mrs. Piper's stream-of-consciousness rumor about a man with a ferocious air and a potential pick-axe.
That is what the Victorian legal system formally preserves as the record of a man's life. Gossip. Fear. Misheard words.
What you're all describing is a novel that holds satire and tragedy, comedy and grief, in the same hand simultaneously — and refuses to let any of them cancel the others out.
We'll be back after the break to look at how Chancery itself — the court at the centre of it all — functions as an institution, and what it does to the people who fall inside it.

segments.title: Closing: What Remains After the Fog

utterances.text: We've spent this episode moving through fog — legal, moral, domestic.
And I want to close by asking each of you: what remains, when the fog finally lifts?
What does Bleak House leave with us — as an image, as a feeling, as a verdict on the world it describes?
Caroline, you've always said this novel earns its title in a very particular way. I'd like to start with you.
What stays with me, always, is the image of Ada kneeling beside Richard.
Dickens frames it with extraordinary tenderness — and Esther sees it and records it almost as a painter would.
The passage reads:
"my darling rose, put off her bonnet, kneeled down beside him with her golden hair falling like sunlight on his head, clasped her two arms round his neck, and turned her face to me."
That image — golden hair like sunlight — is Dickens at his most visually precise and his most heartbreaking.
Richard is dissolving. Ada is whole. And she gives herself to him completely anyway.
That is what the novel offers in place of justice. Not rescue — devotion.
Caroline puts her finger on something important there — the novel refuses to offer systemic remedy.
Richard is destroyed not by villainy in the conventional sense but by the perfectly legal operation of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
And Vholes — the novel's finest portrait of professional detachment weaponised — makes that explicit.
He tells Esther, with perfect composure:
"I HAVE carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over to any connexion of Mr. C.'s on any account."
The capital letters on 'HAVE' are Dickens's own — a rare intrusion of typography to convey the absolute self-satisfaction of the man.
Vholes doesn't smooth things over. He simply watches, documents, and bills.
That is the system. And it goes on after Richard is gone.
James is right that the system endures — but I want to push on what the novel offers as a counter-image to it.
Because I think Dickens knows — and this is where he is more radical than he is usually given credit for — that individual devotion is not enough.
Look at the early passage where Jarndyce speaks to Richard and Ada about their future together.
He says: "I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here — don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear! — being in a mind to go through life together."
That phrase — 'afar off' — is repeated twice, and it rings with dramatic irony by the end of the novel.
Jarndyce sees the desirability of their union. What neither he nor they can see is what Chancery will make of Richard.
Good intentions — paternal, tender, genuine — are no insulation from the machinery that the novel anatomises.
And yet — the novel also insists on something that resists that reading. Something Esther alone can see.
There is that extraordinary moment — one of the most haunting in the book — with the handkerchief and the baby at the brickmaker's cottage.
Esther writes — and listen to the sentence, it unfolds like a slow realisation:

"How little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief to look upon the tiny sleeper underneath and seemed to see a halo shine around the child through Ada's drooping hair — how little I thought in whose unquiet bosom that handkerchief would come to lie after covering the motionless and peaceful breast!"
She doesn't know, in that moment, that this handkerchief will travel to Lady Dedlock — will be the thread of connection between worlds the system wants kept separate.
The novel's structure is built from these unknowing acts of tenderness.
That's what Dickens believes in. Not institutions. Not law. Compassionate hands, in the dark.
I don't entirely disagree with Caroline — those acts of compassion are real in the novel, and they move me.
But that handkerchief doesn't save Lady Dedlock. It identifies her. And she dies in the street.
Dickens trusts in those tender connections. I think he also, somewhere, knows their limits.
The great novelists always know more than their consolations admit.
What strikes me, looking at the novel whole, is the sheer patience of its construction.
Every object, every gesture, every handkerchief — it all returns.
Chancery is the anti-structure — it generates perpetual motion without resolution, cost without product.
Dickens sets the warm, connected fabric of human relation directly against that machine. And the machine wins, legally speaking.
But the novel — the fact of the novel existing — is the argument on the other side.
That feels like the right place to rest — the novel itself as a counter-argument to the world it depicts.
The fog endures. Vholes goes on. But Dickens wrote it all down — and that act of witness is not nothing.
My thanks to Caroline Woodcourt, James Blackstone, and Daniel Rosen for a conversation that has been, in the best sense, worth the fog.
This has been Bleak House Unpacked. We'll be back with more — until then, read on.

The furniture, old-fashioned rather than old, like the house, was as
pleasantly irregular. Ada’s sleeping-room was all flowers—in chintz
and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff
courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool
for greater state, on either side of the fire-place. Our sitting-room
was green and had framed and glazed upon the walls numbers of
surprising and surprised birds, staring out of pictures at a real
trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with
gravy; at the death of Captain Cook; and at the whole process of
preparing tea in China, as depicted by Chinese artists. In my room
there were oval engravings of the months—ladies haymaking in short
waists and large hats tied under the chin, for June; smooth-legged
noblemen pointing with cocked-hats to village steeples, for October.
Half-length portraits in crayons abounded all through the house, but
were so dispersed that I found the brother of a youthful officer of
mine in the china-closet and the grey old age of my pretty young
bride, with a flower in her bodice, in the breakfast-room. As
substitutes, I had four angels, of Queen Anne’s reign, taking a
complacent gentleman to heaven, in festoons, with some difficulty;
and a composition in needlework representing fruit, a kettle, and an
alphabet. All the movables, from the wardrobes to the chairs and
tables, hangings, glasses, even to the pincushions and scent-bottles
on the dressing-tables, displayed the same quaint variety. They
agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the
whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a
drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of
rose-leaves and sweet lavender. Such, with its illuminated windows,
softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the
starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its
hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with
the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and
just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything
we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.

“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”

“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”

The door stood open, and we both followed them with our eyes as they
passed down the adjoining room, on which the sun was shining, and out
at its farther end. Richard with his head bent, and her hand drawn
through his arm, was talking to her very earnestly; and she looked up
in his face, listening, and seemed to see nothing else. So young, so
beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through

“Then make it easy for her!” growled the man upon the floor. “I wants
it done, and over. I wants a end of these liberties took with my
place. I wants an end of being drawed like a badger. Now you’re
a-going to poll-pry and question according to custom—I know what
you’re a-going to be up to. Well! You haven’t got no occasion to be
up to it. I’ll save you the trouble. Is my daughter a-washin? Yes,
she IS a-washin. Look at the water. Smell it! That’s wot we drinks.
How do you like it, and what do you think of gin instead! An’t my
place dirty? Yes, it is dirty—it’s nat’rally dirty, and it’s
nat’rally onwholesome; and we’ve had five dirty and onwholesome
children, as is all dead infants, and so much the better for them,
and for us besides. Have I read the little book wot you left? No, I
an’t read the little book wot you left. There an’t nobody here as
knows how to read it; and if there wos, it wouldn’t be suitable to
me. It’s a book fit for a babby, and I’m not a babby. If you was to
leave me a doll, I shouldn’t nuss it. How have I been conducting of
myself? Why, I’ve been drunk for three days; and I’da been drunk four
if I’da had the money. Don’t I never mean for to go to church? No, I
don’t never mean for to go to church. I shouldn’t be expected there,
if I did; the beadle’s too gen-teel for me. And how did my wife get
that black eye? Why, I give it her; and if she says I didn’t, she’s a
Lie!”

Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and
meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers
of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.
Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights. Fog creeping
into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and
hovering in the rigging of great ships; fog drooping on the gunwales
of barges and small boats. Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient
Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog
in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper,
down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of
his shivering little ’prentice boy on deck. Chance people on the
bridges peeping over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog
all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the
misty clouds.

crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great

personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients;

c1:p0.text:
London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.

The trooper, his old recollections awakened by the solitary grandeur
of a great house—no novelty to him once at Chesney Wold—goes up the
stairs and through the chief rooms, holding up his light at arm’s
length. Thinking of his varied fortunes within the last few weeks,
and of his rustic boyhood, and of the two periods of his life so
strangely brought together across the wide intermediate space;
thinking of the murdered man whose image is fresh in his mind;
thinking of the lady who has disappeared from these very rooms and
the tokens of whose recent presence are all here; thinking of the
master of the house upstairs and of the foreboding, “Who will tell
him!” he looks here and looks there, and reflects how he MIGHT see
something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his
hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the
darkness above and below, while he goes up the great staircase again,
blank as the oppressive silence.

Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.

c13:p113.summary: Mr. Jarndyce addresses Richard and Ada, confirming he is glad to have their confidence and that he did contemplate their union as a possibility.
c13:p113.best_quote: When I contemplated these relations between us four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here (don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear!) being in a mind to go through life together. c8:p117.text:
How little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief to look upon the
tiny sleeper underneath and seemed to see a halo shine around the
child through Ada’s drooping hair as her pity bent her head—how
little I thought in whose unquiet bosom that handkerchief would come
to lie after covering the motionless and peaceful breast! I only
thought that perhaps the Angel of the child might not be all
unconscious of the woman who replaced it with so compassionate a
hand; not all unconscious of her presently, when we had taken leave,
and left her at the door, by turns looking, and listening in terror
for herself, and saying in her old soothing manner, “Jenny, Jenny!”
c8:p117.summary: Esther reflects on the handkerchief covering the baby and wonders about its future journey, expressing her hope that the woman's compassion is recognized by the Angel watching over the child and Jenny.
